title: Kubernetes eviction spike triage — scheduler backpressure + image-gc cascade
content:
Summary:

On 2026-03-11 02:14 UTC we observed a sudden cluster-wide spike in pod evictions concentrated on three node pools (general-purpose, batch, and ML-inference). Evictions began after a period of degraded scheduler performance and coincided with elevated kubelet image garbage collection (image-gc) activity on affected nodes. User-facing errors were brief but noticed by multiple downstream services — the web-app saw 5xx spikes for ~6 minutes and a small percentage of background jobs failed and retried.

Hypothesis (initial):
- A cascade where nodes hit ephemeral-storage/image pressure triggered aggressive image-gc, which increased CPU and disk IO on kubelets.
- High kubelet resource usage led to slower node heartbeats and pod-status updates. The scheduler saw increased API latency and internal queuing, resulting in delayed placement and perceived unschedulable states for pending pods. Some controllers interpreted node pressure as sufficient to evict best-effort pods.
- Concurrently a metrics scraping job (prometheus-push on the batch pool) rebooted with a config change that caused a brief I/O storm and elevated disk use.

Timeline (UTC, approximated from logs + monitoring):
- 02:12:22: node-general-34 reports ephemeral-storage pressure (kubelet: eviction manager alerts)
- 02:12:30: image-gc started on node-general-34; CPU ~95% for kubelet process (top of process list)
- 02:12:44: scheduler metrics: pending queue depth increases from baseline 8 -> 120; API server latency p95 1.2s -> 4.8s
- 02:13:05: first pod evicted due to Reason=Evicted, message=The node was low on resource: ephemeral-storage
- 02:13:30: similar symptoms observed on node-batch-07 and node-ml-11; image-gc runs triggered by high disk usage
- 02:14:00: alerts fired: SRE-eviction-spike; on-call paged
- 02:14:20: on-call team ran kubectl top nodes, df -h on affected nodes via kube-ssh jump host
- 02:15–02:18: manual cordon of most-impacted nodes to stop new scheduling; scaled up an extra batch of nodes in general-purpose pool (autoscaler triggered + manual request)
- 02:20:10: observed gradual recovery as image-gc completed and disk drained; by 02:28 cluster metrics near-normal

Immediate mitigation steps executed:
- Cordon: cordon node-general-34, node-batch-07, node-ml-11 to prevent further scheduling onto IO-saturated nodes (kubectl cordon <node>)
- Throttle schedulers: increased scheduler concurrency tuning not feasible in the moment; instead removed low-priority DaemonSets that were contributing to disk pressure on affected nodes (temporary scale-down of local-logging daemonset)
- Scale up: triggered manual node pool scale-up + verified cluster-autoscaler was healthy; added 6 nodes across pools to absorb pending pods
- Eviction triage: increased eviction thresholds on a small window was considered but not changed because it could mask real disk exhaustion; instead prioritized freeing disk by deleting leftover docker image layers on the most impacted nodes via CRI-O cleanup command and restarting kubelet where necessary

Key commands run during incident (for runbook codification):
- kubectl get events --all-namespaces --field-selector reason=Evicted -o wide --watch
- kubectl describe node node-general-34 | egrep -i "eviction|disk|pressure|image"
- ssh jmp@bastion -- sudo journalctl -u kubelet -n 200 --no-pager | grep -i "Image garbage collection"
- crictl images; sudo rm -rf /var/lib/containers/storage/overlay/* (only after verification and safe deletions)
- kubectl cordon node-general-34
- kubectl scale ds local-logger --replicas=0 -n infra-temp

Root cause analysis (current understanding):
- Primary cause: image garbage collection triggered on nodes due to combined factors: outdated GC thresholds in our kubelet config (imageGCHighThresholdPercent too low for current container churn) and a bursty job (prometheus-target-scraper) that temporarily wrote large files to /var/lib/*, pushing nodes over ephemeral-storage pressure.
- Secondary cause: lack of early disk pressure telemetry with sufficient cardinality — our alerting used node allocatable thresholds which reacted only after pressure crossed eviction points.
- Tertiary/systemic cause: some DaemonSets (local log agents and a debugging sidecar) create ephemeral files and were not covered by lifecycle policies; they contributed to the churn.

What went well:
- Pager and on-call rotation routed to the right SREs quickly; we had a single point of coordination and used a dedicated Zoom to keep actions synchronized.
- Node cordon + targeted cleanup prevented broader cluster degradation; autoscaler scaled quickly enough to absorb pending pods once evictions slowed.
- Runbook commands (cordon, describe, crictl) were effective and executed without introducing new failures.

What didn't go well / gaps identified:
- Image GC thresholds are conservative for our workload patterns. The default/older settings are inadequate for bursty ephemeral workloads.
- Lack of early-file-system write-rate metrics and per-daemonset disk usage visibility. We couldn't immediately attribute disk pressure to the prometheus-target-scraper without deeper digging into node-level disk write metrics.
- No automated pre-emptive remediation when image-gc starts to reach high CPU/disk IO (we only alert when eviction imminent).

Immediate follow-up actions (assigned):
- (Asha) Update kubelet config proposal: raise imageGCHighThresholdPercent to 85 and imageGCLowThresholdPercent to 70 on affected node pools. Add to infra PR: github.com/redwood/infra/pull/2310. Due: 2026-03-18.
- (Mateo) Add a Prometheus metric and alert for kubelet image-gc CPU/disk IO spikes and a per-node file system write-rate panel. Due: 2026-03-16.
- (Sofia) Audit DaemonSets and sidecars: produce list of agents that write to /var/lib or /tmp on nodes; recommend size limits or centralize logs via ephemeral volume policies. Due: 2026-03-20.
- (Liam) Create a runbook addition for "eviction spike (image-gc)" including the exact commands above, safe cleanup steps, and escalation path. Due: 2026-03-15.

Longer-term remediation and design ideas:
- Consider implementing an operator that performs safe background image pruning before kubelet GC becomes aggressive; combine with predictive monitoring (if disk write-rate x churn > threshold then preemptively remove stale images)
- Improve per-DS disk quotas using ephemeral volumes where feasible. Explore CSI ephemeral volumes for temporary buffers to avoid polluting host storage.
- Revisit autoscaler and scheduling policies: add a transient buffer pool for bursty workloads (smaller nodes but fast spin up) and tag high-churn workloads to schedule onto those pools.

Runbook changes to be made (short checklist):
- Add step: check "Image GC CPU %" and "kubelet disk IO" to triage checklist
- Add safe cleanup snippet with checksums and safeguards; mark as sensitive and require SRE approval before host-level deletions
- Add guidance for temporary daemonset scale-down and when to uncordon nodes

Open questions / unknowns to resolve:
- Why did the prometheus-target-scraper cause an unexpected filesystem burst? Was this a config change or bug in the scraper? (opened JIRA SRE-7423 to trace config changes)
- Are there any workloads that depend on pre-warmed local images that would suffer if we tune GC more aggressively? Need inventory of such workloads.

References and artifacts:
- Kubernetes events dump: GCS path: gs://redwood-ops-archives/2026-03-11/evictions-nodepool-general/*
- JIRA SRE-7423 (triage ticket)
- GH PR with kubelet config patch: https://github.com/redwood/infra/pull/2310
- Node logs collected: s3://redwood-logs/2026-03-11/node-general-34-kubelet.log

Notes to self:
- Keep this doc as the canonical quick triage for image-gc-driven evictions. Convert to a small k8s-runbook entry once the immediate action items are completed.

End of notes.
